content.value: In early 2026, Parlour Caribbean entered a new phase of ownership. Because TSTT’s acquisition did not include the platform’s original visual identity, the transition became an opportunity to develop a new brand for the marketplace.

The rebrand aimed to support a more efficient, Caribbean-centred e-commerce experience, with shorter delivery times for local goods, integrated online payments, and clearer access to authentic regional products worldwide. Three brand directions were presented; the third was selected as primary, with the first held for possible future use. I also designed select MVP pages for the new Parlour site in support of
’s development of the revised digital experience.

The Gazette is a Caribbean news aggregator and storytelling platform that brings local journalism, culture, and community updates together in one mobile experience.

During my AXXS Digital internship, I designed three features for the app: a mobile-optimised author page for on-the-go reading and discovery; a daily digest of the most relevant news from the past 24 hours; and a daily word game meant to increase organic opens by giving users a reason to launch the app beyond push notifications.

The spiral treatise argues that time does not move in a straight line or a simple circle, but in a spiral: it revisits similar patterns while moving forward, so nothing repeats exactly. Each moment is both new and tied to the past; change happens through repetition, not in spite of it.

A speculative visualization of the individual’s influence on the flow of time, as outlined in the spiral treatise. An afterimage of the viewer modulates between the present and a user-defined delay into the past; delay and modulation speed are adjustable on the controller. The work offers a sense of agency over time while asking how much control we truly have.

In Interaction Experience/Design (third year), we re-examined daily interactions with an everyday device and designed a tangible interface to enhance or replace part of that interaction. I focused on projectors: presenters often point at slides, but those gestures are not responsive; highlighting text, manipulating 3D models, or triggering embedded media still requires reaching the host computer or a helper.
The controller, initially conceived as a glove, was meant to let presenters interact gesturally with projected content, supporting clearer, more engaging classroom presentations.

In Graphic Design 2 (second year), we designed, built, and published a resource website while avoiding the hyper-commodified look of much of the contemporary web.
Mine shares information about the solar system as a planetarium with the user at the centre. Selecting a planet reveals detail; a control at lower left switches to a comparison of orbital speeds.

content.value: Orbit speed comparison
Bottom-left switch compares planetary orbital periods from a bird’s-eye view.

Planets move far faster than in reality so orbits read on screen (~35 s for Earth at 60 FPS, roughly 900,000× real speed). Inner planets outpace outer ones, but ratios are compressed (Mercury vs Earth, Neptune vs Earth). Speed also varies slightly with refresh rate because motion follows animation frames.
Retrospective note: I likely misread orbital periods during build, so the mapping was inaccurate. I believed the simulation at presentation; later review showed otherwise.

In Research Methods for Graphic Design (third year), the course deliverables were double-sided 11″ × 17″ micropublications exploring a research question that could sustain multiple methods and matter to design practice.

After Micropublication 1, I focused on the question: “How can technological advancements in augmented reality enhance the effectiveness of science communication?” It grew from my interest in how emerging tools can reshape how scientific information is shared, combining future-oriented interface design with science communication.

The book opens with dense visual stimuli and gradually reduces complexity until a single note acknowledges that the process is still evolving as my practice grows.

Imagery was sourced from Adobe Stock.
